stem: An 'open economy' is one that __________.
options: Interacts with other countries through trade in goods and services and flows of capital
Has no contact with other countries
solution: An OPEN ECONOMY is one that INTERACTS with OTHER COUNTRIES — through TRADE in GOODS and SERVICES (exports and imports) and through FLOWS of CAPITAL and finance (foreign investment, loans). A CLOSED economy, by contrast, has no such international transactions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'Balance of Payments' (BoP) is __________.
options: A systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world during a period
A record of only the money supply
solution: The BALANCE of PAYMENTS (BoP) is a SYSTEMATIC RECORD of ALL ECONOMIC TRANSACTIONS between the RESIDENTS of a country and the REST of the WORLD during a given period (usually a year). It records trade, services, income flows, and capital movements. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Balance of Payments has two main accounts: the current account and the __________ account.
solution: The BALANCE of PAYMENTS has TWO main accounts: the CURRENT ACCOUNT (recording trade in goods and services, income, and current transfers) and the CAPITAL ACCOUNT (recording flows of capital — foreign investment, loans, and changes in foreign assets and liabilities). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'current account' of the BoP records __________.
options: Exports and imports of goods and services, income (factor income), and current transfers
solution: The CURRENT ACCOUNT of the BoP records: (1) trade in GOODS (visible trade — exports and imports); (2) trade in SERVICES (invisible trade — shipping, banking, software, tourism); (3) INCOME (factor income like interest, profits, dividends, and compensation); and (4) CURRENT TRANSFERS (remittances, gifts, grants). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'balance of trade' (trade balance) refers to __________.
options: The difference between the value of exports and imports of goods (visible items) only
The total of all BoP transactions
The difference in services trade only
solution: The BALANCE of TRADE (trade balance) refers ONLY to the difference between the value of EXPORTS and IMPORTS of GOODS (VISIBLE/merchandise items). It is narrower than the current account balance, which also includes services, income, and transfers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The difference between the balance of trade and the current account balance is that the current account also includes __________.
options: Trade in services (invisibles), income, and current transfers
solution: The CURRENT ACCOUNT balance is broader than the BALANCE of TRADE: besides goods (visibles), the current account ALSO INCLUDES trade in SERVICES (INVISIBLES), INCOME (factor income), and CURRENT TRANSFERS (like remittances). The trade balance covers only goods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Invisible' items in the current account refer to __________.
options: Services (like shipping, banking, insurance, tourism, software), plus income and transfers
solution: INVISIBLE items in the current account refer to trade in SERVICES — such as SHIPPING, BANKING, INSURANCE, TOURISM, and SOFTWARE — as well as INCOME flows and TRANSFERS. They are called 'invisible' because, unlike goods, they are not tangible items passing through customs. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'capital account' of the BoP records __________.
options: Transactions that affect a country's foreign assets and liabilities, such as foreign investment, loans and banking capital
solution: The CAPITAL ACCOUNT of the BoP records transactions that AFFECT a country's FOREIGN ASSETS and LIABILITIES — such as FOREIGN INVESTMENT (FDI and portfolio/FII), external LOANS/borrowings, BANKING CAPITAL, and changes in foreign exchange reserves. It captures the financing side of international transactions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'current account deficit' occurs when __________.
options: The value of imports of goods and services (and other current payments) exceeds that of exports and current receipts
The capital account is in surplus
solution: A CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT occurs when a country's TOTAL CURRENT PAYMENTS (imports of goods and services plus income and transfers paid out) EXCEED its total current RECEIPTS (exports plus income and transfers received). The country is spending more on the current account than it earns, and must finance the gap (e.g., through the capital account). So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Autonomous' items in the BoP differ from 'accommodating' items in that autonomous items are __________.
options: Undertaken for their own sake (for profit/economic motives), independent of the BoP position ('above the line')
Undertaken only to balance the BoP
solution: AUTONOMOUS items ('above the line') are BoP transactions UNDERTAKEN for their OWN SAKE — for PROFIT or economic MOTIVES — INDEPENDENT of the country's BoP position (e.g., normal trade and investment). ACCOMMODATING items ('below the line') are undertaken to FINANCE/BALANCE the BoP (e.g., official reserve transactions). A BoP is in 'deficit' or 'surplus' based on autonomous items. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'foreign exchange rate' is __________.
options: The price of one currency in terms of another currency
The rate of interest on foreign loans
solution: The FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATE is the PRICE of ONE CURRENCY in TERMS of ANOTHER — e.g., how many rupees are needed to buy one US dollar (₹/$). It determines the value of a country's currency in international transactions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'flexible' (floating) exchange rate is one that is __________.
options: Determined by the market forces of demand and supply of foreign exchange
Fixed by the government at a constant level
solution: A FLEXIBLE (FLOATING) EXCHANGE RATE is one that is DETERMINED by the MARKET FORCES of DEMAND and SUPPLY of foreign exchange. It rises or falls freely with market conditions, without the government pegging it. (A FIXED exchange rate, by contrast, is set/maintained by the government or central bank.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'fixed' exchange rate system is one in which __________.
options: The exchange rate is officially fixed/pegged by the government or central bank and maintained by intervention
The rate changes every minute in the market
solution: A FIXED EXCHANGE RATE system is one in which the exchange rate is OFFICIALLY FIXED (PEGGED) by the GOVERNMENT or CENTRAL BANK at a particular value and MAINTAINED through INTERVENTION (buying/selling foreign exchange from reserves) to keep the rate at the pegged level. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'managed floating' exchange rate system is one where __________.
options: The rate is largely market-determined but the central bank intervenes at times to prevent excessive fluctuations
solution: A MANAGED FLOATING (dirty float) system is a HYBRID: the exchange rate is LARGELY MARKET-DETERMINED, but the CENTRAL BANK INTERVENES at TIMES (buying/selling foreign exchange) to PREVENT EXCESSIVE FLUCTUATIONS and maintain stability. India follows a managed float. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Depreciation' of a currency (under a flexible exchange rate) means __________.
options: A fall in the value of the domestic currency relative to a foreign currency (more rupees needed per dollar)
A rise in the currency's value
solution: DEPRECIATION of a currency (under a FLEXIBLE rate) means a FALL in the VALUE of the DOMESTIC CURRENCY relative to a foreign one — e.g., the rupee depreciates when MORE RUPEES are needed to buy one DOLLAR (say ₹70/$ to ₹75/$). It makes exports cheaper and imports costlier. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Appreciation' of a currency means __________.
options: A rise in the value of the domestic currency relative to a foreign currency (fewer rupees needed per dollar)
A fall in the currency's value
solution: APPRECIATION of a currency means a RISE in the VALUE of the DOMESTIC CURRENCY relative to a foreign one — e.g., the rupee appreciates when FEWER RUPEES are needed to buy one DOLLAR (say ₹75/$ to ₹70/$). It makes exports costlier and imports cheaper. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Devaluation' differs from depreciation in that devaluation __________.
options: Is a deliberate reduction in the value of a currency by the government under a fixed exchange rate system
Is a market-driven fall under a flexible rate
Is a rise in currency value
solution: DEVALUATION is a DELIBERATE (official) REDUCTION in the VALUE of a currency by the GOVERNMENT/central bank under a FIXED exchange rate system. DEPRECIATION, by contrast, is a MARKET-DRIVEN fall in value under a FLEXIBLE rate. Both lower the currency's value but by different mechanisms. So option 1 is correct.

stem: When the rupee depreciates, Indian exports become __________ and imports become __________.
solution: When the RUPEE DEPRECIATES (loses value), Indian EXPORTS become CHEAPER for FOREIGNERS (each unit of their currency buys more rupees' worth of goods), boosting exports; and IMPORTS become MORE EXPENSIVE for Indians (each import costs more rupees), tending to reduce imports. This can help improve the trade balance. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The demand for foreign exchange arises from __________.
options: The need to pay for imports, to invest abroad, to travel/study abroad, and to send transfers abroad
solution: The DEMAND for FOREIGN EXCHANGE arises when residents need foreign currency to PAY for IMPORTS, to INVEST ABROAD, to TRAVEL/STUDY abroad, and to SEND TRANSFERS/gifts abroad. (Supply of foreign exchange comes from exports, remittances received, and foreign investment coming in.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The supply of foreign exchange in a country comes from __________.
options: Exports of goods/services, remittances received from abroad, and foreign investment inflows
solution: The SUPPLY of FOREIGN EXCHANGE comes from EXPORTS of goods and services (foreigners pay in foreign currency), REMITTANCES RECEIVED from abroad, and FOREIGN INVESTMENT INFLOWS (FDI and FII coming into the country). These bring foreign currency in, while imports and outflows take it out. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The equilibrium exchange rate under a flexible system is determined where __________.
options: The demand for foreign exchange equals the supply of foreign exchange
solution: Under a FLEXIBLE (floating) system, the EQUILIBRIUM EXCHANGE RATE is determined where the DEMAND for FOREIGN EXCHANGE EQUALS the SUPPLY of foreign exchange — the market-clearing price of the currency. Shifts in demand or supply move the equilibrium rate. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key ADVANTAGE of a flexible exchange rate system is that __________.
options: The BoP adjusts automatically through exchange-rate movements, and no foreign-exchange reserves are needed to defend a peg
solution: A key ADVANTAGE of a FLEXIBLE exchange rate is that the BALANCE of PAYMENTS ADJUSTS AUTOMATICALLY through EXCHANGE-RATE MOVEMENTS (a deficit causes depreciation, which boosts exports and curbs imports), and the central bank does NOT need to hold large FOREIGN-EXCHANGE RESERVES to DEFEND a peg. A drawback is greater uncertainty/volatility. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A key ADVANTAGE of a fixed exchange rate is that it __________.
options: Provides stability and certainty in international transactions, encouraging trade and investment
solution: A key ADVANTAGE of a FIXED exchange rate is that it provides STABILITY and CERTAINTY in international transactions — traders and investors know the exchange rate in advance, which ENCOURAGES TRADE and INVESTMENT by reducing exchange-rate risk. A drawback is that maintaining the peg requires reserves and policy discipline. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Foreign Direct Investment' (FDI) differs from 'Foreign Portfolio Investment' (FII) in that FDI involves __________.
options: A lasting interest and control in an enterprise (e.g., setting up or acquiring a business), whereas FII is investment in financial assets like shares/bonds without control
solution: FOREIGN DIRECT INVESTMENT (FDI) involves a LASTING INTEREST and a degree of CONTROL/management in an enterprise — e.g., a foreign firm SETTING UP or ACQUIRING a business. FOREIGN PORTFOLIO INVESTMENT (FII) is investment in FINANCIAL ASSETS (shares, bonds) WITHOUT control, and is more liquid and volatile ('hot money'). So option 1 is correct.

stem: If a country has a deficit in its current account, it can be financed by __________.
options: A surplus (net inflow) on the capital account, e.g., borrowing or attracting foreign investment
solution: A CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT can be FINANCED by a SURPLUS (net INFLOW) on the CAPITAL ACCOUNT — by BORROWING from abroad or ATTRACTING FOREIGN INVESTMENT (FDI/FII), or by drawing down foreign exchange reserves. The overall BoP must balance, so a current account gap is matched by capital account flows (and reserve changes). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The foreign exchange reserves of a country are held by the __________.
solution: The FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES of a country (foreign currencies, gold, SDRs, etc.) are held by the CENTRAL BANK — the RESERVE BANK of INDIA (RBI) in India. These reserves are used to intervene in the forex market, defend the currency, and meet international payment obligations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Under a managed float, to prevent the rupee from depreciating too much, the RBI would __________.
options: Sell foreign exchange (dollars) from its reserves, increasing the supply of dollars
solution: To PREVENT the RUPEE from DEPRECIATING too much, the RBI would SELL FOREIGN EXCHANGE (DOLLARS) from its RESERVES in the market. This INCREASES the SUPPLY of dollars (and demand for rupees), supporting the rupee's value and limiting its fall. (To prevent excessive appreciation, it would buy dollars instead.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rise of India's software and IT services exports has strengthened which part of its BoP?
options: The invisibles (services) in the current account
Foreign exchange reserves being drawn down
solution: The rise of India's SOFTWARE and IT SERVICES EXPORTS has strengthened the INVISIBLES (SERVICES) component of the CURRENT ACCOUNT — earning large amounts of foreign exchange from service exports. Along with remittances, this has helped offset India's deficit in visible (goods) trade. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Remittances sent home by Indians working abroad are recorded in the BoP under __________.
options: Current transfers in the current account
The balance of trade in goods
solution: REMITTANCES sent home by Indians working abroad are recorded under CURRENT TRANSFERS in the CURRENT ACCOUNT (they are unilateral transfers, received without any quid pro quo). India is one of the world's largest recipients of remittances, which support the current account. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'nominal exchange rate' differs from the 'real exchange rate' in that the real exchange rate __________.
options: Adjusts the nominal rate for the price levels (relative prices) of the two countries
Is the same as the interest rate
solution: The NOMINAL EXCHANGE RATE is the simple rate at which one currency exchanges for another. The REAL EXCHANGE RATE ADJUSTS the nominal rate for the PRICE LEVELS (RELATIVE PRICES) of the two countries — it measures the ratio at which goods of one country exchange for goods of another, reflecting international competitiveness. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): A depreciation of the domestic currency can help reduce a trade deficit. Reason (R): Depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, tending to raise exports and lower imports. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — a DEPRECIATION can help REDUCE a TRADE DEFICIT. R is TRUE and correctly EXPLAINS A: depreciation makes EXPORTS CHEAPER (for foreigners) and IMPORTS DEARER (for residents), tending to RAISE EXPORTS and LOWER IMPORTS — which narrows the trade deficit. So R is the correct explanation of A. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall balance of payments (autonomous transactions) is said to be in 'deficit' when __________.
options: Autonomous receipts (inflows) fall short of autonomous payments (outflows), requiring financing by reserves/accommodating items
solution: The overall BoP (on AUTONOMOUS transactions) is in DEFICIT when AUTONOMOUS RECEIPTS (inflows) FALL SHORT of AUTONOMOUS PAYMENTS (outflows). This gap must be FINANCED by ACCOMMODATING items — chiefly a drawdown of FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES or official borrowing. A surplus is the opposite. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The trade in goods being in deficit while the overall current account is in surplus (or smaller deficit) is possible because __________.
options: Strong earnings from invisibles (services, remittances) can offset the deficit in goods trade
Goods and services are the same
solution: A GOODS TRADE DEFICIT can coexist with a current-account SURPLUS or a SMALLER current-account deficit because STRONG EARNINGS from INVISIBLES — SERVICES (like IT/software exports) and REMITTANCES — can OFFSET the deficit in VISIBLE goods trade. India often shows this pattern. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches BoP terms?
options: Current account → goods, services, income, transfers; Capital account → foreign investment, loans, reserves; Trade balance → goods only
Current account → only loans; Capital account → only goods; Trade balance → services only
Current account → reserves only; Capital account → transfers only
solution: The correct matches are: CURRENT ACCOUNT → GOODS, SERVICES, INCOME, and TRANSFERS; CAPITAL ACCOUNT → FOREIGN INVESTMENT, LOANS, and RESERVE/banking capital; TRADE BALANCE → GOODS ONLY (visibles). So option 1 correctly identifies what each records. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The foreign exchange market is the market where __________.
options: Currencies of different countries are bought and sold
Only shares of companies are traded
solution: The FOREIGN EXCHANGE MARKET is the market where CURRENCIES of DIFFERENT COUNTRIES are BOUGHT and SOLD (exchanged for one another). Its participants include banks, firms, traders, and central banks, and the exchange rate is the price at which currencies trade. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Revaluation' of a currency (under a fixed exchange rate) means __________.
options: A deliberate increase in the value of a currency by the government
A reduction in value by the government
solution: REVALUATION is a DELIBERATE (official) INCREASE in the VALUE of a currency by the GOVERNMENT/central bank under a FIXED exchange rate system — the opposite of DEVALUATION (a deliberate decrease). It corresponds to appreciation but is a policy action rather than a market outcome. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A depreciation of the domestic currency, other things equal, tends to make the current account __________.
options: Improve (as exports rise and imports fall), though the effect may take time (J-curve)
solution: A DEPRECIATION tends to IMPROVE the CURRENT ACCOUNT because EXPORTS RISE (cheaper for foreigners) and IMPORTS FALL (dearer for residents). However, the improvement may take TIME — initially the account can worsen before improving (the J-CURVE effect) because volumes adjust slowly while import bills rise. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A country running a persistent current account deficit is essentially __________.
options: Spending more than it earns on current transactions, and hence borrowing from (or selling assets to) the rest of the world
solution: A country with a PERSISTENT CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT is essentially SPENDING MORE than it EARNS on current transactions (importing more than it exports, net). To finance this, it must BORROW from the REST of the WORLD or SELL ASSETS to foreigners (capital inflows) — accumulating external liabilities over time. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rupee is said to be 'fully convertible on the current account' meaning that __________.
options: Rupees can be freely converted into foreign currency for current-account transactions (trade, services, remittances)
The rupee cannot be exchanged at all
Only the government can hold foreign currency
solution: 'FULL CONVERTIBILITY on the CURRENT ACCOUNT' means that the rupee can be FREELY CONVERTED into FOREIGN CURRENCY (and vice versa) for CURRENT-ACCOUNT transactions — imports, exports, services, travel, and remittances — without government restriction. India has current-account convertibility but only partial capital-account convertibility. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a component of the SUPPLY of foreign exchange but NOT the demand for it?
solution: EARNINGS from EXPORTS bring foreign currency INTO the country, so they are part of the SUPPLY of foreign exchange (not demand). Payments for imports, Indian tourists abroad, and Indian firms investing abroad all require BUYING foreign exchange, so they are sources of DEMAND. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Under a flexible exchange rate, if Indians' demand for imports rises, the rupee will tend to __________.
options: Depreciate (as demand for foreign exchange rises)
solution: Under a FLEXIBLE rate, if Indians' demand for IMPORTS RISES, the DEMAND for FOREIGN EXCHANGE (dollars to pay for imports) INCREASES. This raises the price of foreign currency in rupees, so the RUPEE tends to DEPRECIATE (its value falls). So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Hot money' (volatile portfolio capital flows) can be a problem for an economy because __________.
options: It can flow out suddenly, causing sharp currency depreciation and financial instability
It has no effect on the currency
solution: 'HOT MONEY' — VOLATILE PORTFOLIO (FII) capital flows — can be a problem because it can FLOW OUT SUDDENLY in response to changing sentiment or returns, causing SHARP CURRENCY DEPRECIATION, stock-market falls, and FINANCIAL INSTABILITY. Unlike FDI, it is not tied to real assets and can reverse quickly. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The balance of payments, as an accounting statement, must always __________.
options: Balance overall (total credits equal total debits), because of double-entry bookkeeping and accommodating items
solution: As an ACCOUNTING STATEMENT using DOUBLE-ENTRY BOOKKEEPING, the BoP must ALWAYS BALANCE overall — total CREDITS equal total DEBITS. Any imbalance in autonomous transactions is offset by ACCOMMODATING items (changes in reserves/official financing). So a 'BoP deficit' or 'surplus' refers to autonomous items, not the overall balance. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Gold and foreign currency assets held by the central bank are part of __________.
solution: GOLD and FOREIGN CURRENCY ASSETS held by the CENTRAL BANK (RBI), along with SDRs and the reserve position in the IMF, make up the country's FOREIGN EXCHANGE (OFFICIAL) RESERVES. These reserves are used for intervention in the forex market and to meet international obligations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A stronger (appreciating) rupee benefits which group the most?
options: Importers and those making payments abroad (imports and foreign travel become cheaper)
solution: A STRONGER (APPRECIATING) RUPEE benefits IMPORTERS and those MAKING PAYMENTS ABROAD — since fewer rupees are needed per dollar, IMPORTS and FOREIGN TRAVEL/study become CHEAPER. It hurts EXPORTERS (their goods become dearer abroad) and those converting foreign remittances into rupees (they get fewer rupees). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Trade in goods is called 'visible' trade because __________.
options: Goods are tangible items that physically cross borders and can be seen/recorded at customs
solution: Trade in GOODS is called 'VISIBLE' trade because goods are TANGIBLE items that PHYSICALLY CROSS BORDERS and can be SEEN and RECORDED at CUSTOMS. Trade in services is 'INVISIBLE' because it does not involve a physical product passing through customs. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If the capital account has a large surplus but the current account has a deficit, the country is __________.
options: Financing its current account deficit through net capital inflows (foreign investment and borrowing)
solution: If the CAPITAL ACCOUNT has a large SURPLUS (net inflows) while the CURRENT ACCOUNT is in DEFICIT, the country is FINANCING its current account deficit through NET CAPITAL INFLOWS — foreign investment (FDI/FII) and borrowing. The capital inflows supply the foreign exchange needed to cover the current account gap. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The main disadvantage of a flexible exchange rate system is that it __________.
options: Can be volatile and uncertain, creating risk for traders and investors
solution: The main DISADVANTAGE of a FLEXIBLE exchange rate is that it can be VOLATILE and UNCERTAIN — the rate can swing sharply with market sentiment, creating EXCHANGE-RATE RISK for TRADERS and INVESTORS and complicating planning. (This uncertainty is why many economies prefer a managed float.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: A country's terms of trade improve when __________.
options: The prices of its exports rise relative to the prices of its imports
Import prices rise faster than export prices
solution: A country's TERMS of TRADE IMPROVE when the PRICES of its EXPORTS RISE RELATIVE to the prices of its IMPORTS — meaning each unit of exports can buy more imports. This benefits the country, as it gets more imported goods for a given volume of exports. So option 1 is correct.

stem: An 'open economy' is one that:
options: interacts (trades and has financial dealings) with other countries
solution: An open economy interacts with other countries through trade in goods and services and financial flows.

stem: The 'Balance of Payments' (BoP) is:
options: a systematic record of all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world in a period
solution: The BoP is a systematic record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a period.

stem: The 'current account' of the BoP records:
options: trade in goods and services, income and current transfers
solution: The current account records trade in goods and services, factor income and current transfers (like remittances).

stem: The 'capital account' of the BoP records:
options: transactions in financial assets — foreign investment, loans and borrowing
solution: The capital account records transactions in financial assets — foreign investment, loans and borrowing between countries.

stem: The 'balance of trade' (trade balance) refers to:
options: the difference between the value of exports and imports of GOODS (visible trade)
solution: The balance of trade is the difference between the value of exports and imports of goods (visible trade).

stem: Trade in goods is called 'visible' trade because:
options: goods are tangible/physical items that can be seen crossing borders
solution: Trade in goods is 'visible' because goods are tangible items that can be seen physically crossing borders.

stem: 'Invisible' items in the current account refer to:
options: trade in services, income and transfers (which are intangible)
solution: Invisibles are the intangible items — trade in services, factor income and transfers — as opposed to visible goods.

stem: The current account also includes, beyond the trade balance:
options: trade in services (invisibles), net income and net current transfers
solution: Beyond the goods trade balance, the current account includes trade in services (invisibles), net income and net current transfers.

stem: Remittances sent home by Indians working abroad are recorded in the BoP under:
solution: Remittances are recorded in the current account as current transfers (an invisible receipt).

stem: A 'current account deficit' occurs when:
options: the total outflow on current account (imports + payments) exceeds the total inflow (exports + receipts)
solution: A current account deficit occurs when current-account outflows (imports and payments) exceed inflows (exports and receipts).

stem: A country running a persistent current account deficit is essentially:
options: borrowing from (or drawing on the savings of) the rest of the world
solution: A persistent current account deficit means the country is spending more than it earns abroad, effectively borrowing from the rest of the world.

stem: 'Autonomous' items in the BoP differ from 'accommodating' items in that autonomous items are:
options: undertaken for their own sake (independent of the BoP position), while accommodating items are done to cover the imbalance
solution: Autonomous items are undertaken for their own sake (e.g., trade, investment for profit), while accommodating items are official financing done to cover the BoP imbalance.

stem: The overall balance of payments (autonomous transactions) is said to be in 'deficit' when:
solution: The BoP is in deficit when autonomous outflows exceed autonomous inflows, requiring accommodating finance (drawing down reserves).

stem: The balance of payments, as an accounting statement, must always:
options: balance (the accounts sum to zero, with accommodating items covering any autonomous imbalance)
solution: As an accounting statement, the BoP always balances overall, with accommodating (official reserve) transactions offsetting any autonomous imbalance.

stem: The 'foreign exchange rate' is:
options: the price of one currency in terms of another
solution: The foreign exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g., rupees per dollar).

stem: The foreign exchange market is the market where:
solution: The foreign exchange market is where currencies are bought and sold against one another.

stem: A 'flexible' (floating) exchange rate is one that is:
options: determined by market forces of demand and supply for the currency
solution: A flexible (floating) exchange rate is determined by the market forces of demand and supply for the currency.

stem: A 'fixed' exchange rate system is one in which:
options: the exchange rate is fixed/pegged by the government or central bank
solution: A fixed exchange rate is pegged/fixed by the government or central bank at a particular value.

stem: A 'managed floating' exchange rate system is one where:
options: the rate is largely market-determined but the central bank intervenes to moderate fluctuations
solution: Under managed floating, the rate is largely market-determined but the central bank intervenes to smooth excessive fluctuations.

stem: 'Depreciation' of a currency (under a flexible rate) means:
options: a fall in the value of the currency in terms of foreign currency (market-driven)
solution: Depreciation is a market-driven fall in the value of a currency relative to a foreign currency.

stem: 'Appreciation' of a currency means:
options: a rise in the value of the currency in terms of foreign currency
solution: Appreciation is a rise in the value of a currency relative to a foreign currency.

stem: 'Devaluation' differs from depreciation in that devaluation:
options: is a deliberate reduction in the value of a currency by the government under a fixed exchange rate
solution: Devaluation is a deliberate official reduction in a currency's value under a fixed exchange rate, whereas depreciation is market-driven.

stem: 'Revaluation' of a currency (under a fixed rate) means:
options: a deliberate official increase in the currency's value
solution: Revaluation is a deliberate official increase in a currency's value under a fixed exchange rate.

stem: A depreciation of the domestic currency, other things equal, tends to make the current account:
solution: Depreciation tends to raise exports and lower imports, improving the current account (trade balance).

stem: The demand for foreign exchange arises from:
options: imports of goods/services, investment abroad, and remittances/transfers out
solution: Demand for foreign exchange arises from imports, investing abroad, travel/education abroad and transfers out.

stem: The supply of foreign exchange comes from:
options: exports of goods/services, foreign investment inflows, and remittances received
solution: Supply of foreign exchange comes from exports, foreign investment inflows and remittances/receipts from abroad.

stem: The equilibrium exchange rate under a flexible system is determined where:
options: the demand for and supply of foreign exchange are equal
solution: The equilibrium exchange rate is where the demand for foreign exchange equals its supply.

stem: Under a flexible exchange rate, if Indians' demand for imports rises, the rupee will tend to:
solution: Higher import demand raises the demand for foreign exchange, causing the rupee to depreciate.

stem: A key ADVANTAGE of a flexible exchange rate system is that:
options: the rate adjusts automatically to correct BoP imbalances (no need to hold large reserves)
solution: A flexible rate adjusts automatically to correct BoP imbalances, so the central bank need not hold large reserves to defend a peg.

stem: The main disadvantage of a flexible exchange rate system is that it:
options: can be volatile/unstable, creating uncertainty for trade and investment
solution: A flexible rate can be volatile and unstable, creating uncertainty for international trade and investment.

stem: A key ADVANTAGE of a fixed exchange rate is that it:
options: provides stability and certainty for international trade and investment
solution: A fixed exchange rate provides stability and certainty, which encourages international trade and investment.

stem: Under a managed float, to prevent the rupee from depreciating too much, the RBI would:
options: sell foreign exchange (from its reserves) to increase its supply and support the rupee
solution: To support the rupee, the RBI would sell foreign exchange from its reserves, increasing the supply of foreign currency and raising the rupee's value.

stem: The foreign exchange reserves of a country are held by the:
solution: Foreign exchange reserves are held by the central bank (the RBI in India).

stem: Gold and foreign currency assets held by the central bank are part of:
options: the country's foreign exchange reserves (official reserves)
solution: Gold and foreign currency assets held by the central bank make up the country's official foreign exchange reserves.

stem: 'Foreign Direct Investment' (FDI) differs from 'Foreign Portfolio Investment' (FII) in that FDI involves:
options: a lasting interest and control in an enterprise (setting up/acquiring a business)
solution: FDI involves a lasting interest and management control in an enterprise, whereas portfolio investment (FII) is buying financial assets without control.

stem: 'Hot money' (volatile portfolio capital flows) can be a problem because it:
options: can flow out suddenly, destabilising the currency and financial markets
solution: Hot money can flow out suddenly, destabilising the currency and financial markets — a risk of short-term portfolio flows.

stem: If a country has a current account deficit, it can be financed by:
options: a capital account surplus (foreign investment/borrowing) or drawing down foreign exchange reserves
solution: A current account deficit can be financed by a capital account surplus (foreign investment/borrowing) or by drawing down reserves.

stem: If the capital account has a large surplus but the current account has a deficit, the country is:
options: financing its current account deficit through capital inflows (foreign investment/borrowing)
solution: A capital account surplus financing a current account deficit means the country is covering its excess spending abroad through capital inflows.

stem: The 'nominal exchange rate' differs from the 'real exchange rate' in that the real exchange rate:
options: adjusts the nominal rate for the price levels (relative prices) of the two countries
solution: The real exchange rate adjusts the nominal exchange rate for the relative price levels of the two countries, reflecting relative competitiveness.

stem: A country's terms of trade improve when:
options: the prices of its exports rise relative to the prices of its imports
solution: Terms of trade improve when export prices rise relative to import prices, so a given quantity of exports buys more imports.

stem: The rupee being 'fully convertible on the current account' means that:
options: it can be freely converted to foreign currency for current transactions (trade, travel, remittances)
solution: Full current-account convertibility means the rupee can be freely converted for current transactions like trade, travel and remittances.

stem: The trade in goods being in deficit while the overall current account is in surplus is possible because:
options: strong invisibles (services exports, remittances) can more than offset the goods trade deficit
solution: Strong invisibles — services exports (like IT) and remittances — can offset a goods trade deficit, giving a current account surplus or smaller deficit.

stem: Assertion (A): A depreciation of the domestic currency can help reduce a trade deficit. Reason (R): Depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, tending to raise exports and lower imports. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: by making exports cheaper and imports dearer, depreciation tends to raise exports and cut imports, reducing the trade deficit.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Open Economy Macroeconomics'?
options: In an open economy, a country's transactions with the world are recorded in the balance of payments (current and capital accounts), and the exchange rate — fixed, flexible or managed — links its economy to others, with important effects on trade and the BoP
solution: The chapter concludes that in an open economy, a country's transactions with the rest of the world are recorded in the balance of payments (current and capital accounts), and the exchange rate — under fixed, flexible or managed regimes — links the economy to others, with important effects on trade and the balance of payments.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Open Economy Macroeconomics' is that:
options: Countries should never trade with each other

An OPEN ECONOMY interacts with the rest of the world through trade and capital flows, all recorded in the BALANCE of PAYMENTS — split into the CURRENT ACCOUNT (goods, services/invisibles, income, transfers) and the CAPITAL ACCOUNT (foreign investment, loans, reserves); international transactions require exchanging currencies at the FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATE, which may be FLEXIBLE (market-determined, with appreciation/depreciation), FIXED (pegged, with devaluation/revaluation), or MANAGED FLOATING; exchange-rate changes affect exports and imports and hence the trade balance, and a current account deficit is financed through the capital account or reserves — so open-economy links are central to a country's income, prices and policy
The exchange rate has no effect on trade
The balance of payments never needs to balance
solution: The chapter's overall message is that an OPEN ECONOMY interacts with the REST of the WORLD through TRADE (in goods and services) and CAPITAL FLOWS, all recorded in the BALANCE of PAYMENTS (BoP). The BoP is split into the CURRENT ACCOUNT (recording GOODS, SERVICES/INVISIBLES, INCOME, and TRANSFERS) and the CAPITAL ACCOUNT (recording FOREIGN INVESTMENT, LOANS, and reserve/banking capital). International transactions require exchanging currencies at the FOREIGN EXCHANGE RATE, which may be FLEXIBLE (market-determined by demand and supply, moving through APPRECIATION and DEPRECIATION), FIXED (officially PEGGED, adjusted through DEVALUATION/REVALUATION), or MANAGED FLOATING (largely market-determined with central-bank intervention). EXCHANGE-RATE CHANGES affect EXPORTS and IMPORTS — a depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, helping the trade balance — and a CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT must be FINANCED through the CAPITAL ACCOUNT or by drawing on foreign exchange RESERVES. Thus open-economy linkages are CENTRAL to a country's income, prices, and macroeconomic policy. So the overall message is option 2.
